label: HMRC policy paper · 29 October 2026
title: Landlords and savers: new 24%, 44% and 49% income tax rates from 6 April 2027
summary: Budget 2026 introduced separate income tax rates for property and savings income. From 6 April 2027 they will be 24% basic, 44% higher and 49% additional rate.
body:
Budget 2026 introduced separate income tax rates for property income and savings income. HMRC set out the change in a policy paper published on 29 October 2026. If you let out property, or you have significant interest from savings, this will affect your tax bill from the 2027 to 2028 tax year.

The new rates from 6 April 2027

  • Property income: property basic rate 24%, property higher rate 44%, property additional rate 49%.
  • Savings income: savings basic rate 24%, savings higher rate 44%, savings additional rate 49%.

These rates apply from 6 April 2027, the start of the 2027 to 2028 tax year. Your 2025 to 2026 tax return, due by 31 January 2027, and the current 2026 to 2027 tax year are not affected.

Who is affected

  • Individual landlords who receive rental profits personally, including those who own property jointly with a spouse or partner.
  • Savers whose interest is taxable, for example interest above any tax-free allowance they have or interest outside an ISA.

The policy paper deals with income tax rates. If your property is held through a limited company, talk to us about how the change applies to you.

Why it matters for planning

Because property and savings income will have their own rates, the same amount of profit could cost more tax in 2027 to 2028 than it would have if taxed at the ordinary income tax rates. It is worth looking at this now, while there is still a full tax year before the change.

  • Budget for higher bills: if you pay tax through Self Assessment, your balancing payment for 2027 to 2028 and your payments on account could be higher. Plan your cash flow with that in mind.
  • Review ownership and structure: landlords often ask whether they should change how a property is owned, or move it into a company. These decisions can have capital gains tax and Stamp Duty Land Tax costs, so get advice before doing anything.
  • Use tax-free wrappers: savers may want to review how much of their savings sit inside ISAs.
  • Making Tax Digital: landlords already in Making Tax Digital for Income Tax should make sure their software and records are up to date, as quarterly updates will feed into these new calculations.

What happens next

HMRC has said these measures are being legislated following the Budget. We will keep clients updated once detailed guidance on how the new rates interact with allowances and reliefs is published.

If you are a landlord and want to understand what the new property rates could mean for your tax bill, get in touch. We can review your rental figures and talk through your options before April 2027.
